look_here_first: Native Texas signalgrass with comparatively BIG ovoid pointed spikelets (~4.5–6 mm), borne singly or in pairs along several ascending side branches of a terminal panicle. Check the lower glume (around half to two-thirds of spikelet length), cross-veined lower lemma and tough, transversely wrinkled upper fertile lemma. Whole-plant overview alone is not enough for confirmation.

best_field_traits: Warm-season native Texas grass; often an annual tuft of soft relatively broad foliage.
Terminal panicle generally with multiple alternate ascending principal branches, often 4 or more.
Spikelets distinctively large for this 3-way comparison, about 4.5–6 mm long; single or paired at branch nodes.
Lower glume often reaches near middle to ~two-thirds spikelet, unlike much smaller basal glumes of U. fusca or U. reptans.
Very short stalked spikelets, lower floret male/sterile and upper floret fertile; upper fertile lemma firm and finely cross-wrinkled.
True ligule and sheath anatomy need macro confirmation and should never be fabricated from habitat overview.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Panicle close-up with ascending branches in frame
Mature 4.5–6 mm ovoid spikelet beside mm scale
Attached lower glume measuring about half to two-thirds spikelet length
Dissect lower male floret versus upper tough fertile lemma
Leaf collar, ligule, blade width with ruler
Full habit including basal rooted tuft
crew_field_check: START WITH THREE SIGNALGRASS HEADS: U. fusca has tight rather chunky spikelet clusters; U. reptans forms a much more delicate spreading narrow-branched head; U. texana has larger (~4.5–6 mm) spikelets along alternate ascending branches. These silhouettes HELP, but reliable separation depends on measuring mature spikelets and the proportion of the LOWER GLUME.
Measure actual mature spikelet(s) with a millimeter ruler.
Inspect lemma/glume or true ligule ONLY where detailed pixels or a collected macro are actually available.
Record uncertain grass to genus, don't force the species from one photo.

comparisons.key_distinctions: U. fusca has plumper smaller ~2.4–3 mm spikelets in generally shorter densely packed flowering branches. U. reptans has tiny ~1.5–2.5 mm spikelets and loose slender branches plus decumbent growth. Other Paniceae may look similar; do not confirm solely from whole clump or 'signalgrass' common name. In this one existing wide photograph, detailed spikelets are too small to verify.
